CORS Misconfiguration Checker

Sends six real HTTP GET requests to an API URL you choose, each with a different Origin header, then classifies the responses into four well-documented CORS misconfiguration patterns: reflecting an unrelated origin, accepting Origin: null, and two unanchored allow-list bypass shapes (startsWith/endsWith-style string checks with no domain boundary), plus notices for a wildcard-with-credentials combination and a missing Vary: Origin header. Only point it at a system you own or are authorised to test.

1. Run the CLI against your API

Node.js, no dependencies to install:

node check.mjs https://api.example.com/some/endpoint --json

Get check.mjs, probe.mjs, and analyze.mjs from the repo — plain Node, nothing to install. It only ever talks to the URL you pass; nothing goes through this site.

2. Paste the JSON output here

Paste the JSON from step 1 and click Check.

Report

Raw probe responses

ProbeOrigin sentStatusAccess-Control-Allow-OriginAccess-Control-Allow-Credentials

Common questions

What is a CORS misconfiguration and why does it matter?

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser mechanism that lets a server explicitly allow another website to read its responses. A misconfigured server can end up trusting any origin at all, the literal origin "null", or an attacker-registrable domain that happens to satisfy a sloppy string check -- any of which lets an attacker's website read data (sometimes including a logged-in visitor's authenticated data) it should never see.

Why does this need a CLI instead of just checking a URL I type into the page?

Origin is a forbidden request header under the Fetch spec, so a browser tab is never allowed to set it to anything other than the page's own real origin -- that restriction is part of what CORS protects. Only a non-browser HTTP client, like the CLI here (or curl), can send the crafted Origin headers this check depends on. Run the CLI, then paste its JSON output here for a rendered report.

Is it safe to run this against a URL?

It sends six ordinary, unauthenticated GET requests -- nothing here bypasses authentication, reads protected data, or does anything a browser wouldn't also do by visiting the URL with different Origin headers. Only point it at a system you own or are authorised to test, the same rule that applies to any request tool aimed at someone else's server.

Does a clean report mean the API has no CORS issues?

No. This checks four specific, well-documented misconfiguration patterns using six requests -- it is not a full security assessment, does not test authenticated endpoints with real credentials, and cannot see a bypass this tool's four attack probes don't happen to trigger. Treat a clean report as evidence about these specific patterns, not a determination that the API is secure.

Why does one of the six requests send my own origin?

That request is not an attack and echoing it back is never reported as a finding -- allowing your own origin is the correct answer. It is there for the Vary: Origin notice, which is about the caching layer in front of the API rather than the allow-list behind it. On a server whose allow-list works, all four attack origins are correctly rejected, so nothing else in the run would ever show that the response still changes with the request. The sixth request does, and the request that sends no Origin header at all is what tells a dynamic header from a static one: a value that is identical whether or not you send an Origin is the same response for everybody and owes no Vary.

More background: what a reflected-origin CORS misconfiguration actually lets an attacker do.

Already testing with a full web security platform? See how this checker compares to Burp Suite — a six-request CI gate next to an interactive assessment tool, and when each one is the right answer. Testing with plain curl instead? See how this checker compares to sending a crafted Origin header yourself — one curl request finds the obvious reflected-origin bug, but the other three patterns only surface by comparing several requests side by side.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks four specific, well-documented CORS misconfiguration patterns from six requests. It is not a full security assessment, does not send real credentials or test authenticated behaviour, and cannot see a pattern its probes don't happen to trigger. A clean report describes what these six requests found, not a guarantee the target has no CORS issues.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not security advice, and it does not replace a qualified security review or penetration test. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for having authorisation to test any system you point the CLI at. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. This tool is free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. Do not use it as a system of record.

Nothing leaves your browser. The CLI's requests go straight from your machine to the URL you name -- never through this site. The page you're reading now only parses JSON you paste into it locally; nothing is uploaded. The only thing stored is an anonymous local count of which features were used and the day -- no target URLs, no response headers, no account, no tracking cookies, no analytics vendor. Turn it off with the checkbox above.

Free and open source. The code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

Also worth a pass on your CI: GitHub Actions injection checker and pinned actions checker cover a different class of supply-chain and injection risk in the same "read what's actually there, name the exact evidence" shape as this tool, Subresource Integrity checker covers a different tag-and-response evidence class again -- a stale CDN hash rather than a reflected CORS origin -- and Security Headers checker covers a third response-header evidence class: clickjacking protection and Content-Security-Policy strength rather than a reflected Origin, and Supabase RLS exposure checker covers a database-level access-control evidence class again -- whether a table returns real rows, not a response header at all, and GraphQL introspection exposure checker covers a schema-enumeration evidence class again -- whether an unauthenticated introspection query reveals the full query/mutation surface, not a response header or a database table, and Regex ReDoS Check covers a denial-of-service class in your own source -- regular expressions that backtrack catastrophically on a crafted string, and JWT Verification Misuse Check finds token handling that decodes without verifying, accepts alg none or signs with a hard-coded secret.

reflected-origin-cors-vulnerability.html.text:
What a reflected-origin CORS misconfiguration lets an attacker do

CORS exists so a server can explicitly opt certain other websites into reading its responses, which browsers otherwise block by default (the same-origin policy). The server does this with the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header. A correct implementation checks the request's Origin header against an explicit allow-list and either echoes back that exact origin (if allowed) or omits the header (if not). A broken implementation just copies whatever Origin it was sent straight into the response -- which looks identical to a correct implementation for a legitimate visitor, and only shows up when someone sends an origin that was never meant to be allowed.

Why this is exploitable, not just untidy

A browser will only expose the response body to the requesting page's JavaScript when the server's CORS headers say it's allowed. If the server reflects any origin, that permission is meaningless -- every website on the internet passes the check. Combine that with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true (which tells the browser to send the visitor's cookies along with the cross-origin request) and an attacker's page can silently request your API in the background, using the victim's own session, and read back whatever a logged-in user could see.

Three ways the same bug shows up

PatternWhat triggers itWhy it's exploitable
Reflects any originOrigin: an unrelated made-up domainNo allow-list check is happening at all
Accepts Origin: nullOrigin: nullA sandboxed iframe or a data: URI sends this automatically -- an attacker needs no domain of their own
Unanchored allow-listOrigin: a domain crafted to pass a naive startsWith/endsWith string checkAn attacker can register a real domain that passes the check but isn't actually related to the allowed site

Check for all three automatically

The checker on this site sends six real requests -- these three plus a baseline and a wildcard-with-credentials check -- and reports exactly which pattern, if any, your API shows, with the response header that proves it. The requests come from a Node CLI you run yourself against a system you own or are authorised to test; the browser page only renders a report you paste in, since a browser tab cannot set the Origin header itself.

This is evidence from those six requests, not a full security assessment -- see the checker and its disclaimer for what it does and doesn't cover, and verify against a proper security review before treating a clean report as final.

← Back to the checker

No warranty. This page is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not security advice, and it does not replace a qualified security review or penetration test. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Free and open source. MIT licence -- support is entirely optional.

vs-burp-suite.html.text:
← CORS misconfiguration checker

This checker vs. Burp Suite

Burp Suite, from PortSwigger, is one of the best-known tools in web application security. It is a testing platform built around an intercepting proxy: you route a browser through it, watch and modify the traffic, and replay or vary individual requests by hand with tools such as Repeater and Intruder. PortSwigger distributes it in a free Community Edition and in paid editions that add automated vulnerability scanning, and it publishes a large body of free learning material — including its Web Security Academy topic on CORS, which is where several of the attack shapes this checker probes for are documented in the first place.

That is a much bigger job than the one this page does, and a different shape of job. This checker is a single zero-dependency Node command. It sends six ordinary GET requests to one URL you name, each with a different Origin header, and classifies the responses into four named CORS misconfiguration patterns — a reflected unrelated origin, an accepted Origin: null, and two unanchored allow-list bypass shapes — plus notices for wildcard-with-credentials and a dynamic Access-Control-Allow-Origin missing Vary: Origin. It names the exact response header behind each finding and exits non-zero when a danger-severity finding is produced. It has no proxy, no browser integration, no scanner, and no opinion about any vulnerability class other than CORS.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Assess a whole web application, explore it interactively, work through authenticated flows, and chain findings together. Burp Suite or a comparable web security testing platform — none of that is something this checker attempts.
Find out whether this one endpoint reflects an arbitrary origin, accepts Origin: null, or has an unanchored allow-list check. This checker — one command, six requests, a report naming the header that proves it.
Gate a deploy in CI on a CORS regression, unattended, on a runner with no GUI and no licence key. This checker — zero dependencies, exit code 1 on a danger finding.
Build a working proof of concept for a bug report, or test how a finding behaves with real session credentials. Burp Suite — this checker sends unauthenticated GETs only and produces no exploit.
Scan for the wide catalogue of web vulnerability classes that are not CORS at all. Burp Suite's scanner, in the editions that include it, or another scanner — this checker looks at CORS and nothing else.
Understand the attack classes before testing for them. PortSwigger's Web Security Academy CORS material is free and excellent; this checker's own background page covers the same three patterns in short form.

These compose rather than compete. A reasonable setup is this checker wired into your own CI against your own staging environment, so an allow-list change that reintroduces a reflected origin turns a build red the day it lands, and a real assessment — with Burp Suite or with a person you hire — for everything a six-request check cannot see. Neither one makes the other redundant.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or Burp Suite?

They do different jobs, and most people testing an API seriously will end up wanting both. Burp Suite, from PortSwigger, is a general-purpose web security testing platform built around an intercepting proxy: you route a browser through it, explore the application, and replay or vary individual requests by hand with tools like Repeater and Intruder, with automated vulnerability scanning available in its paid editions. It covers a very broad catalogue of web vulnerability classes, of which CORS is one. This checker covers nothing but CORS. It is a single zero-dependency Node command that sends six GET requests with different Origin headers to one URL, classifies the responses into four named misconfiguration patterns plus two notices, names the exact response header behind each, and exits non-zero on a danger finding. Reach for Burp Suite when you are assessing a whole application, working through authenticated flows, or building a proof of concept. Reach for this when you want that one CORS question answered repeatably, in CI, on a machine with no GUI and no licence.

Burp Suite has a free edition. What does this add?

Being free is not the difference, and this page does not claim it is: PortSwigger publishes a free Community Edition of Burp Suite, and its Web Security Academy material on CORS attacks is free to read as well. The differences that matter here are shape and scope. Burp Suite is a desktop application you install, launch, and drive interactively through a proxy; automated and scheduled scanning is what its paid editions are for. This checker is one command with no install beyond Node, no licence key, no proxy configuration, and no interactive step, so it runs unattended on a CI runner and gates a deploy on its exit code. And it is deliberately narrow: it answers one question about one endpoint rather than surveying an application, which is why its output is short enough to read in full every time.

If a scanner already covers CORS, why run a CORS-only tool?

Because the two are used at different moments. A full assessment happens occasionally, by a person, against a build of an application. A CORS misconfiguration is usually introduced by a one-line change to an allow-list months later, and the cheapest place to catch that is a check that runs on every deploy of your own staging environment and costs nothing to run again. That is what this tool is shaped for: six requests, a deterministic classification, an exit code. It does not replace an assessment, and a clean report from it is evidence about six specific requests, not a determination that the API is secure.

Is this page affiliated with PortSwigger or Burp Suite?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by PortSwigger, and Burp Suite is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not. The description of Burp Suite on this page is drawn from PortSwigger's own public site; check it there for what any edition currently includes.

Only point either tool at a system you own or are authorised to test. That rule is unchanged by which one you pick.

← Back to the CORS misconfiguration checker

vs-checking-cors-by-hand.html.text:
← CORS misconfiguration checker

This checker vs. checking CORS by hand with curl

Every developer testing CORS already has this move: send one request with an attacker-shaped Origin header and read what comes back. 

curl -sI -H "Origin: https://evil.example" https://api.example.com/v1/account

If Access-Control-Allow-Origin comes back as https://evil.example, that one request already proved the server reflects an arbitrary origin. For that specific, most-obvious bug, a single manual request is enough. The problem is the other three patterns this checker looks for are not visible in any single response -- they only show up when you compare how the server answers several differently-crafted requests against each other, which is where a one-off curl call stops being enough evidence.

Where one request stops being enough

What you're trying to catchOne curl request by handThis checker's CLI
A server that reflects any origin at all, with no allow-list logic. Works. This is the one pattern a single crafted request reliably shows. Also finds it, in the same run as the three below.
An allow-list built on unanchored startsWith/endsWith string matching. Invisible to the obvious test -- an origin like https://evil.example is correctly rejected by this exact bug. Confirming it needs two specifically-crafted origins (https://api.example.com.attacker-controlled.invalid and https://evil-api.example.com) plus a same-origin control, compared side by side. Sends both bypass shapes and the control automatically, and diffs the three responses for you.
The literal origin Origin: null being accepted, exploitable from a sandboxed iframe. Easy to forget -- it is not a URL, so it does not occur to most people testing the reflected-origin case to also send it. Sent on every run, whether or not you thought to ask for it.
A dynamic Access-Control-Allow-Origin missing Vary: Origin, a shared-cache cross-visitor leak risk. Requires sending two requests with different origins and diffing both full header sets -- not something a single curl -I shows. Compares the baseline and same-origin probes automatically and flags the gap as a notice.
Re-running the same six-request comparison after every deploy. Six separate curl calls, six read-backs, every time -- not something most people repeat unprompted. One command, exit-code gateable in CI.

A single well-aimed curl request is still the fastest way to confirm the obvious reflected-origin case, and this checker's own CLI is not doing anything a request tool couldn't -- it is sending the same kind of requests curl would, just six of them in the specific shapes that expose the other three patterns, and comparing the results for you instead of leaving the comparison to be done, and remembered, by hand.

Common questions

Can't I just run curl with a fake Origin header myself?

Yes, for the most obvious case: curl -H "Origin: https://evil.example" -I https://api.example.com/endpoint and reading Access-Control-Allow-Origin back will catch a server that reflects any origin at all. What one request cannot show you is a comparison -- an unanchored allow-list bug only reveals itself when you compare how the server responds to several differently-crafted origins side by side, which is six requests and six diffs done by hand, every time you want to re-check.

What does comparing several requests catch that one curl call does not?

An allow-list built on startsWith or endsWith string matching instead of an exact host comparison. A single request with an obviously fake origin like https://evil.example is correctly rejected by this exact bug, so it looks safe. The bug only surfaces against a crafted origin such as https://api.example.com.attacker-controlled.invalid (passes a naive startsWith check) or https://evil-api.example.com (passes a naive endsWith check) -- and confirming it is a real bug rather than a coincidence means sending both shapes plus a same-origin control and comparing all three responses, not reading any one of them alone.

Is Origin: null something I would remember to test by hand?

It is easy to skip, because it is not a real website's origin -- it is the literal string "null", which browsers send from a sandboxed iframe, a redirected request, or a file:// page, and which a security-minded allow-list might accept by mistake precisely because it looks like the absence of an origin rather than an attacker-controlled one. Nothing about testing the obvious reflected-origin case prompts you to also try this one; it has to be a request you remember to craft separately.

How would I notice a missing Vary: Origin header just by eyeballing responses?

You would not, from a single request -- a missing Vary: Origin looks identical to a present one until you send two requests with different Origin headers and diff the two response header sets for whether Access-Control-Allow-Origin actually changed. Noticing that a shared cache in front of the API could now serve one visitor's allowed origin back to a different visitor requires holding both responses in view at once, which is exactly the kind of side-by-side comparison a single manual curl call does not produce.

Is this page making a live comparison against a tool or company?

No. This page describes a manual method every developer already has -- sending a request with curl (or Postman, or a browser devtools replay) and reading the response headers by eye. It names no competing product or company. The checker's own CLI requests go straight from your machine to the URL you name, never through this site.

Already testing with a full web security platform instead of raw curl? See how this checker compares to Burp Suite. More background: what a reflected-origin CORS misconfiguration actually lets an attacker do.

Only point either method at a system you own or are authorised to test.
